To overlay means to place or spread something on top of something else so that it forms a layer — a new surface that covers the thing below, either completely or partially. The original thing doesn't go away; it stays right there underneath. What changes is that something new is now lying on top of it.

Picture a glass table. Now you spread a printed tablecloth on top of it. The tablecloth overlays the table — it rests on the surface, covers it, and changes how it looks, but the glass table is still there underneath. That's the heart of this word: you add a new layer on top of something that already exists.

Overlay always involves two things:

  • The base — the original thing that already exists
  • The layer — the new thing placed on top

When you overlay something, you are the one doing the placing. The layer always goes on top of the base — not inside it, not beside it, not replacing it. Just resting on its surface.

"The workers overlaid the old wooden floor with marble tiles."
→ The wooden floor is still there underneath; you just can't see it because the marble covers it.

"Artists in ancient times overlaid wooden objects with thin sheets of gold."
→ The wood is the base; the gold is the layer on top.

"She overlaid the blueprint with a transparent sheet so she could draw notes on it without marking the original."
→ The blueprint is the base; the transparent sheet is the layer.

This is one of the most common places you'll encounter "overlay" today.

"The navigation app overlays turn-by-turn directions onto the live map."
→ The map is the base; the directions are a new layer placed on top. Both are visible at the same time.

"The video editor overlaid subtitles onto the film."
→ The film is the base; the subtitle text is the layer placed on top.

"The game overlays a health bar and mini-map onto the game world."
→ The game world is the base; the interface elements sit on top of it.

"She overlaid her company logo onto the slide background."

In all these cases, the base still exists — you can often still see it — and the new layer sits on top.

"Overlay" is also used non-physically. Here, something intangible — like a mood, emotion, or quality — is described as sitting on top of an experience and shaping how it feels.

"A heavy silence overlaid the room after he delivered the news."
→ The silence wasn't something you could touch, but it settled on top of everything in the room and dominated it.

"Grief overlaid every moment of the celebration, making it bittersweet."
→ The grief is like an invisible layer sitting on top of the celebration, coloring the whole experience.

"A thin veneer of politeness overlaid what was clearly a hostile relationship."
→ The politeness is a surface layer — thin and unconvincing — placed on top of the hostility underneath.

The idea is the same as always: something sits on top of something else and dominates or colors it, even if the original thing is still there.
A key nuance: the original remains

This is what separates "overlay" from "replace." When you overlay something, you cover it — but it is still there.

"They overlaid the old stone walls with modern plaster."
→ The old stone walls are still behind the plaster. They haven't been demolished — just covered.

This is why "overlay" is the right word when you want to express that something new has been added on top, not that the original has been destroyed or removed.

These words are close but not the same.

Cover is the most general word. You can cover a pot with its lid, cover yourself with a blanket, or cover a page with writing. "Overlay" is more specific: it suggests a layer — something that lies flat and spread out on the surface of something else, like a coating, a film, or a sheet.

Overlap means two things extend into each other's shared space — like two circles that cross into each other's area. Overlap suggests shared territory between two things beside each other. But when you overlay something, one thing is placed squarely on top of the other. The new layer rests on the base; they don't cross into each other from the side.

So: overlapping = two things sharing space side by side; overlaying = one thing placed directly on top of another.
Overlay vs. Overlie — don't confuse them

There are two different verbs: overlay and overlie. They look related and are related, but they are different in an important way.

To overlie means to lie on top of something. The subject is what's already sitting on top — no one is actively placing it; it's just described as being there.
→ "Gold leaf overlies the wood." (The gold is already there on top of the wood.)

To overlay means to actively place something on top of something else. Someone is doing the action.
→ "Workers overlaid the wood with gold leaf." (Someone put the gold leaf there.)

Overlay = active. Someone places the layer.
Overlie = descriptive. Something is simply resting on top.

Here's the tricky part: the past tense of overlie is overlay — the same spelling. "The rock overlay the fossil for millions of years." Here, "overlay" is the past tense of overlie, not overlay. This confuses even experienced writers, so just be aware: if you see "overlay" used to describe something that is already on top of something (not actively placed), it's probably the past tense of overlie.

FormExample
  • Present: overlay / overlays → "She overlays the image with bold text."
  • Past: overlaid → "They overlaid the floor with new tiles."
  • Past participle: overlaid → "The floor had been overlaid with tiles."
  • Present participle: overlaying → "He is overlaying the design with a new pattern."

One common mistake: the past tense is overlaid, not overlayed. The -ay ending becomes -aid in the past tense (just like "pay → paid" and "lay → laid").

To overlay something is to place something new on top of it as a layer — covering its surface, while the original thing remains underneath. This can be:

  • Physical: gold sheets laid onto wood, tiles laid over old floors, a film placed on a map
  • Digital: graphics placed on top of images, subtitles on video, data placed on top of a map
  • Figurative: a mood or feeling that lies on top of an experience and shapes how it feels

The three core ideas that define this word: there is an existing base; something new is placed on top as a layer; and the original still exists underneath, even if it's now hidden.
